Dogmatic

dawg-MAT-ik -- from Greek dogma, 'opinion, belief,' from dokein, 'to think, to seem': a dogmatic person treats one opinion as beyond question. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Dogmatic is rigidly uncompromising about one's own principles or beliefs.

No amount of new evidence could move the committee's most dogmatic member off his original position.

Worked Example

Even after three separate studies contradicted his original claim, the researcher continued presenting it at conferences exactly as before, refusing to revise a single sentence of his argument.

Dogmatic describes someone who treats their own belief as beyond question -- ignoring three separate contradicting studies rather than adjusting the claim even slightly is exactly that kind of rigid certainty.

How Dogmatic Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

opinionated

opinionated: having strong opinions that one is quick to express

inflexible

inflexible: unwilling to change or bend under any circumstances

Antonyms

open-minded

open-minded: willing to consider new ideas or arguments

flexible

flexible: willing to change or adapt

How Strong Is It? — opinionated → inflexible → dogmatic

opinionated vs. dogmatic

opinionated vs. dogmatic: Opinionated simply means holding strong views and stating them often, while dogmatic adds the sharper criticism that someone refuses to even entertain the possibility they're wrong.

inflexible vs. dogmatic

inflexible vs. dogmatic: Inflexible pushes further than dogmatic by emphasizing total rigidity in any situation, not just a refusal to update one particular belief.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — dog-/dok-

root — dog-/dok-: opinion, belief; to think, to seem (Greek dogma, from dokein)

suffix — -ic

suffix — -ic: characteristic of (Greek -ikos)

Put it together

Put it together: Dogmatic comes from Greek dogma, 'opinion or belief,' which traces to dokein, 'to think, to seem' -- the same ancient root, more distantly, behind orthodox, since orthodox comes from orthos ('straight, right') plus doxa ('opinion'), also rooted in dokein.

Use the root in a new word: orthodox

Use the root in a new word: orthodox: The chef trained for years in classic, orthodox French technique before inventing his own style.
